title: India's 9.1% Pay Hikes Hide a Widening Split Over AI Skills, Aon Finds
excerpt: Aon's survey of 1,200+ employers projects average hikes of 9.1% for 2027, but 37% of firms plan 10% or more while a quarter — including much of IT services — stay under 8% as AI-role premiums jump about 10%.
body:
• Indian employers are projected to raise salaries by an average of 9.1% in 2027, barely above the 9% given in 2026, according to Aon's Annual Salary Increase and Turnover Survey of more than 1,200 organisations across 45 industries.
  • The average hides a widening split: nearly 37% of companies plan hikes of 10% or more, while one in four — including many IT and IT-enabled services firms — will give less than 8%.
  • Pay premiums for AI, machine learning and data science roles have risen about 10% from 2025, and new sectors such as data centres, semiconductors and quick commerce are offering the richest increments.
  • With inflation projected at 5.1% in 2027, up from 4.3% in 2026, employees outside scarce-skill roles face raises that shrink in real terms.

India's salary hikes are holding steady on average — and splitting sharply underneath. Employers are expected to give average increases of 9.1% in 2027, in line with the actual 9% increase in 2026, according to Aon's Annual Salary Increase and Turnover Survey for India 2026-27, which analysed data from more than 1,200 organisations across 45 industries. The India Today analysis of the survey found the gap is being driven by skills: as firms chase scarce AI and data talent, pay is skewing toward those roles and away from everyone else.

A Two-Speed Increment Season

The distribution of hikes has polarised. Almost 37% of companies are looking at giving hikes of 10% or more, compared with just 12% last year. Around 38% plan hikes in the 8-10% range, down from 72% last year — the middle is emptying out. At the other end, one in four companies, 25%, up from 16%, will give hikes of less than 8%, a group that includes IT and IT-enabled services firms. Sector projections underline the spread: non-banking financial companies lead at 10.1%, followed by energy at 9.9% and real estate and infrastructure at 9.8%, while technology consulting and services sits at the bottom at 6.6%, according to The Hindu BusinessLine's report of the survey. Life sciences and funds and asset management are projected at 9.6% each, global capability centres at 9.4% and banking at 8.5%.

The AI Premium

The clearest dividing line is artificial intelligence. Talent premiums for AI, machine learning and data science roles have risen approximately 10% from 2025 as companies invest in agentic AI, and established adoption of AI productivity tools rose from 46.1% in 2025 to 56% in 2026, across every job cluster measured. Around 60% of employers are prioritising employee upskilling. Amit Kumar Otwani, Associate Partner for Talent Solutions in India at Aon, said divergence has increased as new sectors such as data centres, semiconductors and quick commerce offer higher increments, and that hikes are now a function of niche and critical skills whose holders can command a premium even in sectors where hiring is slowing.

"Employers are increasingly focused not only on how much they spend, but where that investment can deliver the greatest workforce and business value."

— Roopank Chaudhary, Partner and Rewards Consulting Leader, Aon India

Attrition and the Real-Terms Squeeze

Competition for talent is intensifying even as budgets stay flat. Overall attrition rose to 18% in 2026 from 16.2% in 2025, and involuntary attrition rose to 4% from 3.4% amid layoffs, alongside high voluntary attrition as scarce-skill employees field outside offers. Roopank Chaudhary, Partner and Rewards Consulting Leader for Talent Solutions in India at Aon, said strong domestic consumption, sustained investment and export growth continue to support business confidence, allowing employers to invest in talent while maintaining cost discipline. Employers are also preparing for the Wage Code: 65.4% say they are already compliant and 20.9% expect to comply within six months, while 42.8% anticipate payroll cost increases of at least 1%.

For employees, the practical reading is blunt. A 9.1% headline average against projected inflation of 5.1% in 2027 — up from 4.3% in 2026 — means real gains concentrate in the roles companies are fighting over: AI, data, and the new data-centre and semiconductor build-out. Workers in generalist roles, and in the quarter of companies planning sub-8% hikes, will see pay that barely keeps pace with prices. The leverage, the survey suggests, now sits with demonstrable scarce skills — and with the willingness to move, as the 18% attrition rate shows many already are.
